entry.title: A crime has been committed… in a sudoku!

link.title: A crime has been committed… in a sudoku!

entry.content:
Image by Veer Mickey Shah retrieved from Unsplash

Murdoku is an ingenious logical deduction puzzle that blends the spatial constraints of classic Sudoku with a murder mystery narrative (Whodunit).

Unlike traditional Sudoku, where we fill cells with numbers from 1 to 9, in Murdoku we must place a set of suspects and the victim on a map representing the crime scene (rooms, furniture, and objects) to ultimately deduce who the killer is.

General rules of Murdoku

To solve a Murdoku case, five fundamental physical and logical rules must be respected:

  1. One person per row and column: Each row and each column of the grid can contain at most one person (whether a suspect or the victim). Once someone’s position is confirmed, that row and column are completely blocked for everyone else.
  2. The map as evidence: The board is not neutral; it is divided into colored areas or rooms and contains specific elements such as chairs, sofas, tables, plants, TVs, or bookshelves (depending on the crime to solve).
  3. Strict compliance with clues: Each suspect has their own clue (in addition to potential global clues) dictating their position relative to other suspects, rooms, or objects (e.g., “south of X”, “to the left of Y”, “the only person on a sofa”).
  4. The crime rule (Identifying the culprit): Once all people are placed on the map satisfying the clues and row/column constraints, the killer is the person who is alone with the victim in the same room or colored region.
  5. Interaction with furniture and objects:
    • A person cannot be in a cell containing a table, plant, TV, barrel, bookshelf (or other similar objects).
    • A person can be in a cell containing a bed or an armchair.

The night of the crime

A violent storm cut off the mansion’s power supply at midnight. Amidst the darkness, a brief struggle shattered the silence of the house. When the emergency lights turned on minutes later, the lifeless body of Victor lay on the floor.

The inspector in charge has cordoned off the property and recorded the positions of the nine people present in the mansion (the victim and eight suspects). Cross-referencing the floor plans of the various rooms, from the basement to the bathroom, with the statements of those present, the goal is to pinpoint each individual’s position with mathematical precision to uncover who cornered the victim. The floor plan of the mansion is as follows:

Case file

  • Victim: Victor (V)
  • Suspects: Alex (A), Bruno (B), Carolina (C), Diana (D), Eva (E), Fabian (F), Gabriel (G), Hector (H)

Case clues

  • Clue 1 (Suspect A): Was not next to a table.
  • Clue 2 (Suspect B): Was in the bottom row.
  • Clue 3 (Suspect C): Was next to a bookshelf.
  • Clue 4 (Suspect D): Was east of Bruno. Was not next to a table.
  • Clue 5 (Suspect E): Was in the basement. Was not next to the TV.
  • Clue 6 (Suspect F): Was alone. Was sitting in an armchair.
  • Clue 7 (Suspect G): Was in the bathroom.
  • Clue 8 (Suspect H): Was next to a table.
  • Clue 9 (Victim V): Was alone with the killer.
  • Global Clue 1: There was exactly one person in bed.
  • Global Clue 2: There was no empty room.
  • Global Clue 3: There were exactly two people sitting in an armchair.

Challenge solution

By solving the logical feasibility model, the location of each suspect and the victim is determined as follows:

Solving the crime:

  • Location of the victim ($V$): Victor is located in cell (7,2) (red circle), inside the basement.
  • Culprit: The killer is Eva (blue circle), as she is the only person in the basement with the victim.

The puzzle can be formulated as a binary linear optimization model, do you dare to try it?

The solution will be shown soon.

Source code

The Python code to read the board, clues, and solve the optimization model using the corresponding solver will be published soon in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: The harmony of digits in solving Kakuro

link.title: The harmony of digits in solving Kakuro

entry.content:
Image by Mohamed Marey retrieved from Unsplash

Kakuro (popularly known as the number crossword) is one of the world’s most popular logic puzzles. It combines the spatial placement of Sudoku with classic arithmetic combinatorics.

Unlike conventional Sudoku, where the objective focuses on digit permutations, Kakuro requires analyzing numerical combinations that sum to an exact amount without repeating any digit in the same row or column.

Despite its apparent mathematical complexity, the game does not require supernatural skills, but rather deductive logical reasoning, data structuring, and basic combinatorics.

Formal description of the problem

The game is played on a grid made up of white cells (empty), black cells (blocked), and colored cells (with clues):

  1. You must fill each white cell with a single digit from 1 to 9 inclusive.
  2. Each continuous block of white cells (horizontal or vertical) has an associated sum clue located in the colored cell immediately to its left or above.
  3. The sum of the numbers in each block must equal exactly the assigned clue.
  4. No digit can be repeated within the same continuous block of white cells.

To determine the correct assignment, we have the following initial board:

Would you like to try solving it logically before looking at its mathematical formulation?

Challenge solution

By solving the Kakuro, the following unique digit assignment is obtained:

Result: There is a unique valid solution that simultaneously satisfies horizontal and vertical sums without repeating digits in each block.

This puzzle can be formulated as a binary linear optimization model, do you dare to try it?

To solve Kakuro systematically and automatically, we can formulate it as a binary linear optimization model.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{R}\): Set of rows.
  • \(\mathcal{C}\): Set of columns.
  • \(\mathcal{W} \subset \mathcal{R} \times \mathcal{C}\): Set of white cells.
  • \(\mathcal{K} = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}\): Set of possible numerical values.
  • \(\mathcal{H}\): Set of horizontal blocks. For each \(h \in \mathcal{H}\), \(\mathcal{S}_h \subset \mathcal{W}\) is the set of its cells.
  • \(\mathcal{V}\): Set of vertical blocks. For each \(v \in \mathcal{V}\), \(\mathcal{S}_v \subset \mathcal{W}\) is the set of its cells.

Parameters

  • \(V_h\): Target sum of cell values in row block \(h \in \mathcal{H}\).
  • \(V_v\): Target sum of cell values in column block \(v \in \mathcal{V}\).

Decision variables

  • \(x_{rck} = 1\) if white cell \((r,c) \in \mathcal{W}\) takes digit \(k \in \mathcal{K}\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Since we are solving a logical feasibility problem, the objective function can be a constant:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

We now define the rules of Kakuro as linear constraints:

Each white cell must contain exactly one digit:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} x_{rck} = 1 \quad \forall (r,c) \in \mathcal{W}\]

Satisfying sums in horizontal blocks:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{S}_h} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} k x_{rck} = V_h \quad \forall h \in \mathcal{H}\]

Uniqueness of digits in horizontal blocks:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{S}_h} x_{rck} \leqslant 1 \quad \forall h \in \mathcal{H}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Satisfying sums in vertical blocks:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{S}_v} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} k x_{rck} = V_v \quad \forall v \in \mathcal{V}\]

Uniqueness of digits in vertical blocks:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{S}_v} x_{rck} \leqslant 1 \quad \forall v \in \mathcal{V}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Variable domains

\[x_{rck} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall (r,c) \in \mathcal{W}, \; \forall k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Source code

entry.title: Killer Sudoku, the empty board challenge that math can solve

link.title: Killer Sudoku, the empty board challenge that math can solve

entry.content:
Image by Mohamed Marey retrieved from Unsplash

Killer Sudoku (or Sudoku Killer) is one of the most exciting and challenging variants of classic Sudoku. It combines the spatial positioning logic of traditional Sudoku with the basic arithmetic of Kakuro.

At first glance, the board can seem intimidating because there are no starting numbers filled in the grid. Instead, the board is divided into groupings of cells or “cages”, marked with colored or dashed lines, each featuring a small number in its top-left corner.

Myth says you need to be a mathematical genius to solve the most advanced levels in your head, but the reality is that Killer Sudoku doesn’t require supernatural skills, it requires deductive logical reasoning, data structuring, and knowing the Rule of 45 (the sum of numbers 1 through 9 in any row, column, or block is always 45).

Formal description of the problem

The goal of Killer Sudoku is the same as in regular Sudoku: fill each row, column, and $3 \times 3$ region once with the numbers from 1 to 9. The difference lies in how those numbers are deduced.

The specific rules of Killer Sudoku are as follows:

  1. You must fill all rows, columns, and $3 \times 3$ regions with numbers from 1 to 9, just like in standard Sudoku.
  2. Each cell is part of a cage, indicated by borders of different colors or dashed lines.
  3. The sum of the numbers inside each cage must equal the value shown in its top-left corner.
  4. Numbers cannot be repeated within the same cage.
  5. Numbers cannot be repeated within the same row, column, or $3 \times 3$ region.

To find the correct solution, we have the following initial board:

Would you like to try solving it logically before looking at its mathematical formulation?

Challenge solution

By solving the Killer Sudoku applying classic constraints along with the cage sums, the following unique assignment matrix is obtained:

Result: As in any well-designed Sudoku, there is a unique solution that simultaneously satisfies the exact cage sums and uniqueness across rows, columns, and quadrants.

This problem can be formulated as a binary linear optimization model, do you dare to try it?

To solve Killer Sudoku systematically and automatically, we can formulate it as a binary linear optimization model.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}\): Set of rows.
  • \(\mathcal{J} = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}\): Set of columns.
  • \(\mathcal{K} = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}\): Set of numerical values a cell can take.
  • \(\mathcal{B} = \{1, 2, \dots, 9\}\): Set of $3 \times 3$ blocks or regions. Cells \((i,j)\) in block \(b\) belong to subset \(R_b\).
  • \(\mathcal{C}\): Set of cages.
  • \(\mathcal{S}_c\): Set of cells \((i,j)\) belonging to cage \(c \in \mathcal{C}\).
  • \(V_c\): Target value (sum) of cage \(c \in \mathcal{C}\).

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ijk} = 1\) if cell at row \(i \in \mathcal{I}\) and column \(j \in \mathcal{J}\) takes numerical value \(k \in \mathcal{K}\), and \(0\) otherwise.

Since we are solving a logical feasibility problem, the objective function can simply be a constant:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

We now define the rules of Classic Sudoku and those specific to the Killer variant as linear constraints:

Each cell must contain exactly one numerical value:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} x_{ijk} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Each value must appear exactly once per row:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} x_{ijk} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Each value must appear exactly once per column:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} x_{ijk} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{J}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Each value must appear exactly once per $3 \times 3$ block:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(i,j) \in R_b} x_{ijk} = 1 \quad \forall b \in \mathcal{B}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

The sum of cell values in each cage must equal its target value:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_c} \sum_{k \in \mathcal{K}} k \cdot x_{ijk} = V_c \quad \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\]

Numbers cannot repeat within the same cage (although this is often implied by classic Sudoku rules for small cages, it is strictly part of the Killer rules):

\[\displaystyle \sum_{(i,j) \in \mathcal{S}_c} x_{ijk} \leqslant 1 \quad \forall c \in \mathcal{C}, \; k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Variable domains

\[x_{ijk} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}, \; \forall k \in \mathcal{K}\]

Source code

The Python implementation of the optimization model (using libraries such as gurobipy or PuLP) for this post is available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: Solving the Number Sums board using mathematical optimization

link.title: Solving the Number Sums board using mathematical optimization

entry.content:
Image by Cooper Hofmann retrieved from Unsplash

Number Sums is a numeric logic puzzle played on a matrix board. Each row and column features a clue value located in its margins. The goal is to select a subset of numbers from the grid such that the sum of the selected values in each row and column matches all the clues on the board exactly and simultaneously.

Below is an example board of size $8 \times 8$:

Can you select the correct numbers before checking the binary programming model?

Challenge solution

The combination of selected numbers (circled) that satisfies all row and column sums is:

The Number Sums game can be formulated directly as a binary linear optimization problem.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, \dots, R\}\): Set of rows of the matrix.
  • \(\mathcal{J} = \{1, \dots, C\}\): Set of columns of the matrix.

Parameters

  • \(A_{ij} \in \mathbb{Z}^+\): Number located in cell $i \in \mathcal{I}, j \in \mathcal{J}$.
  • \(R_i \in \mathbb{Z}^+\): Target sum for row $i \in \mathcal{I}$.
  • \(C_j \in \mathbb{Z}^+\): Target sum for column $j \in \mathcal{J}$.

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\): Binary variable equal to $1$ if the number in cell $(i,j) \in \mathcal{I} \times \mathcal{J}$ is selected, and $0$ if discarded.

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

Required sum in each row:

\[\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} A_{ij} x_{ij} = R_i \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}\]

Required sum in each column:

\[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} A_{ij} x_{ij} = C_j \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Variable domains:

\[x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; j \in \mathcal{J}\]

entry.title: Building bridges with linear optimization, the Hashi puzzle

link.title: Building bridges with linear optimization, the Hashi puzzle

entry.content:
Image by Kjell-Jostein Sivertsen retrieved from Unsplash

Hashi (short for Hashiwokakero, which means building bridges) is a popular logic puzzle played on a rectangular grid featuring islands represented by numbered circles. The goal of the game is to connect all the islands using bridges while satisfying a set of formal constraints:

  1. Alignment: Bridges can only be drawn horizontally or vertically between islands aligned in the same row or column, with no other islands in between.
  2. Connection capacity: At most two bridges can be built between any pair of neighboring islands.
  3. No intersection: Bridges cannot cross each other.
  4. Fixed degree: Each island must have a total number of connected bridges exactly equal to the number indicated inside it.
  5. Single connected network: All islands must end up connected within a single connected component (a continuous transportation network).

Below is an example of a Hashi board consisting of $52$ islands:

Would you like to try connecting the islands logically before checking the solution and the optimization model formulation?

Challenge solution

The complete network of bridges that solves the board above is given by:

The Hashi puzzle can be formulated as a mixed-integer linear programming model using a network flow approach to guarantee full connectivity.

To structure the model mathematically, we represent the islands as a set of vertices and the potential connections between adjacent islands as edges.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{V} = \{1, \dots, N\}\): Set of islands on the board.
  • \(\mathcal{E} = \{(i,j) : i < j\}\): Set of valid segments (without intermediate islands) between horizontally or vertically aligned islands.
  • \(\mathcal{C}\): Set of pairs of perpendicular segments that intersect in the grid space, i.e., $((i,j), (k,l)) \in \mathcal{C}$.

Parameters

  • \(d_i\): Numerical degree fixed inside island $i \in \mathcal{V}$.
  • \(N\): Total number of islands ($N = \vert{}\mathcal{V}\vert{}$).

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ij} \in \{0, 1, 2\}\): Number of bridges built on segment $(i,j) \in \mathcal{E}$.
  • \(y_{ij} \in \{0, 1\}\): Binary variable equal to $1$ if at least one bridge exists between $i$ and $j$, and $0$ otherwise.
  • \(f_{ij} \geqslant 0, \; f_{ji} \geqslant 0\): Directed auxiliary flow circulating between $i$ and $j$ to ensure network connectivity.

Since this is a mathematical feasibility problem, the objective function is arbitrary:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

We define the formal constraints of the model below:

Numerical degree of each island:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{j : (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} x_{ij} + \sum_{j : (j,i) \in \mathcal{E}} x_{ji} = d_i \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V}\]

Relationship between bridges (\(x_{ij}\)) and binary connection indicator (\(y_{ij}\)):

\[y_{ij} \leqslant x_{ij} \leqslant 2 y_{ij} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\]

Prohibition of crossing between orthogonal bridges:

\[y_{ij} + y_{kl} \leqslant 1 \quad \forall ((i,j), (k,l)) \in \mathcal{C}\]

Global network connectivity (Single-Commodity Flow Model):

We fix a root island (for instance, island $1$). The root island acts as a source demanding $N - 1$ units of flow that it distributes to the remaining $N - 1$ islands on the board:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{j : (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}} (f_{ij} - f_{ji}) + \sum_{j : (j,i) \in \mathcal{E}} (f_{ji} - f_{ij}) = \begin{cases} N - 1 & \text{if } i = 1 \\ -1 & \text{if } i \neq 1 \end{cases} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V}\] \[f_{ij} + f_{ji} \leqslant (N - 1) y_{ij} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\]

Variable domains:

\[x_{ij} \in \{0, 1, 2\} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\] \[y_{ij} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\] \[f_{ij}, f_{ji} \geqslant 0 \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{E}\]

Source code

The Python implementation of the optimization model presented in this post is available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: The knight’s perfect tour, challenge chess with linear optimization

link.title: The knight’s perfect tour, challenge chess with linear optimization

entry.content:
Image by servet photograph retrieved from Unsplash

The Knight’s Tour is a classic mathematical and chess problem that consists of moving a knight on an $n \times n$ chessboard so that it visits each and every square exactly once.

There are two main variants of this problem:

  • Closed tour: The knight ends on a square that is one move away from the starting square, forming a complete cycle that could repeat indefinitely.
  • Open tour: The knight visits all squares, but the final square does not allow returning to the starting square in a single move.

This problem has fascinated mathematicians for centuries, from the celebrated Leonhard Euler in the 18th century to modern research in graph theory and Operations Research.

Do you dare to find a complete closed path before checking the solution and its mathematical modeling?

Challenge solution

A valid closed tour on the $8 \times 8$ board is given by the following continuous sequence of $64$ moves:

In total, there are more than 33 trillion tours, of which around 26 trillion allow returning to the initial square.

The Knight’s Tour can be formulated as a Traveling Salesperson Problem on a directed graph, do you dare to try it?

To solve the Knight’s Tour systematically, we can use an integer linear optimization model based on the Miller-Tucker-Zemlin subtour elimination formulation (Miller et al., 1960).

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{V} = \{1, 2, \dots, N\}\): Set of $N = n^2$ board squares ($N = 64$ for an $8 \times 8$ board).
  • \(\mathcal{A} \subset \mathcal{V} \times \mathcal{V}\): Set of directed arcs $(i,j)$ representing valid knight moves between square $i$ and square $j$.

Parameters

  • \(N\): Total number of board squares ($N = 64$).

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ij} = 1\) if the knight moves directly from square $i \in \mathcal{V}$ to square $j \in \mathcal{V}$, and $0$ otherwise.
  • \(u_i \in \{1, \dots, N\}\): Continuous auxiliary variable indicating the visiting order of square $i \in \mathcal{V}$ in the tour sequence.

Since this is a feasibility problem (finding a Hamiltonian cycle in the knight’s movement graph), the objective function is arbitrary:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

We now define the model constraints:

Exactly one outgoing move per square:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{j : (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} x_{ij} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V}\]

Exactly one incoming move per square:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{i : (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}} x_{ij} = 1 \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{V}\]

Subtour elimination (MTZ Formulation):

\[u_i - u_j + N x_{ij} \leqslant N - 1 \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}, \; i \neq 1, \; j \neq 1\]

Variable domains:

\[u_1 = 1\] \[1 \leqslant u_i \leqslant N \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{V}\] \[x_{ij} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall (i,j) \in \mathcal{A}\]

Source code

The Python implementation of the optimization model presented in this post is available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: Beyond 0 and 1, the binary sudoku
entry.content:
Image by Eva Gorobets retrieved from Unsplash

Binary Sudoku (also known as Takuzu or Binairo) is a logic puzzle played on an $n \times n$ grid board, where $n$ is an even number. The goal is to fill all empty cells with only zeros and ones while respecting three fundamental rules:

  1. Balance: Each row and each column must contain exactly the same number of zeros and ones.
  2. Consecutive limit: No more than two identical numbers can be adjacent (neither horizontally nor vertically).
  3. Uniqueness: No two rows and no two columns can be identical.

A Binary Sudoku puzzle starts with some cells already filled with initial values. Below is an example of an $8 \times 8$ board:

Would you like to try solving it logically before looking at its mathematical formulation?

Challenge solution

The solution to the Binary Sudoku presented above is given by:

Binary Sudoku can be formulated as a binary linear optimization model, do you dare to try it?

To explain how to solve Binary Sudoku systematically, we can use a binary linear optimization model. First, we define the elements of the model:

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{R} = \{1, \dots, n\}\): Board rows.
  • \(\mathcal{C} = \{1, \dots, n\}\): Board columns.
  • \(\mathcal{I} \subset \mathcal{R} \times \mathcal{C}\): Set of positions with a fixed initial value.

Parameters

  • \(n\): Board dimension (must be an even number).
  • \(A_{rc} \in \{0, 1\}\): Predetermined value in cell $(r,c) \in \mathcal{I}$.

Decision variables

  • \(x_{rc} = 1\) if the cell at row $r \in \mathcal{R}$ and column $c \in \mathcal{C}$ contains a $1$, and $0$ if it contains a $0$.
  • \(z_{rr'c} \in \{0,1\}\): Auxiliary variable indicating whether row $r \in \mathcal{R}$ and row $r’ \in \mathcal{R}$ differ in column $c \in \mathcal{C}$ ($1 \leqslant r < r’ \leqslant n$).
  • \(w_{cc'r} \in \{0,1\}\): Auxiliary variable indicating whether column $c \in \mathcal{C}$ and column $c’ \in \mathcal{C}$ differ in row $r \in \mathcal{R}$ ($1 \leqslant c < c’ \leqslant n$).

Since we aim to find a valid configuration (feasibility problem), the objective function is arbitrary:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

We now define the Binary Sudoku rules as constraints:

Respect fixed initial cells:

\[x_{rc} = A_{rc} \quad \forall (r,c) \in \mathcal{I}\]

Same number of zeros and ones in each row and column:

\[\displaystyle \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} x_{rc} = \frac{n}{2} \quad \forall r \in \mathcal{R}\] \[\displaystyle \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} x_{rc} = \frac{n}{2} \quad \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\]

At most two consecutive identical digits (no horizontal or vertical trios):

\[1 \leqslant x_{rc} + x_{r,c+1} + x_{r,c+2} \leqslant 2 \quad \forall r \in \mathcal{R}, \; \forall c \in \{1,\dots,n-2\}\] \[1 \leqslant x_{rc} + x_{r+1,c} + x_{r+2,c} \leqslant 2 \quad \forall r \in \{1,\dots,n-2\}, \; \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\]

No two identical rows:

\[z_{rr'c} \geqslant x_{rc} - x_{r'c} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant r < r' \leqslant n, \; \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\] \[z_{rr'c} \geqslant x_{r'c} - x_{rc} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant r < r' \leqslant n, \; \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\] \[\displaystyle \sum_{c \in \mathcal{C}} z_{rr'c} \geqslant 1 \quad \forall 1 \leqslant r < r' \leqslant n\]

No two identical columns:

\[w_{cc'r} \geqslant x_{rc} - x_{rc'} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant c < c' \leqslant n, \; \forall r \in \mathcal{R}\] \[w_{cc'r} \geqslant x_{rc'} - x_{rc} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant c < c' \leqslant n, \; \forall r \in \mathcal{R}\] \[\displaystyle \sum_{r \in \mathcal{R}} w_{cc'r} \geqslant 1 \quad \forall 1 \leqslant c < c' \leqslant n\]

Variable domains

\[x_{rc} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall r \in \mathcal{R}, \; \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\] \[z_{rr'c} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant r < r' \leqslant n, \; \forall c \in \mathcal{C}\] \[w_{cc'r} \in \{0,1\} \quad \forall 1 \leqslant c < c' \leqslant n, \; \forall r \in \mathcal{R}\]

Source code

The Python implementation of the optimization model presented in this post, as well as the instance used in the example, are available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: Dominating the chessboard with queens
entry.content:
Image by Steve A Johnson retrieved from Unsplash

Unlike the famous 8 Queens Problem (where the goal is to place eight queens without them threatening each other), the Queens Domination Problem poses the inverse question from a spatial control standpoint: what is the minimum number of queens needed to attack or guard all squares on a chessboard?

In graph theory, this challenge is equivalent to finding the domination number ($\gamma$) of the queen’s graph. A square is considered “dominated” if it contains a queen or if it is within direct reach of at least one queen (in the same row, column, or diagonal).

Given a standard $8 \times 8$ chessboard, we must determine the smallest possible number of queens that can be deployed so that no empty square is left unattacked.

Would you like to try solving it logically before looking at its mathematical formulation?

Challenge solution

By solving the model with an integer optimization solver like Gurobi, it can be proven that the minimum domination number for an $8 \times 8$ board is 5 queens.

One of the optimal configurations obtained places the queens as shown in the following figure:

How do we translate this coverage of attack lines into a Binary Linear Optimization model?

To model this problem, we define the attack range of a queen from each cell on the board. If we place a queen in cell $(r,c)$, it dominates all cells aligned horizontally, vertically, or diagonally.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, 2, \dots, 8\}\): Board rows.
  • \(\mathcal{J} = \{1, 2, \dots, 8\}\): Board columns.
  • \(\mathcal{A}_{ij} \subset \mathcal{I} \times \mathcal{J}\): Set of cells $(r,c)$ from which a queen would attack cell $(i,j)$ (including cell $(i,j)$ itself). A cell $(r,c) \in \mathcal{A}_{ij}$ if it satisfies any of these conditions:
    • Same row: \(r = i\)
    • Same column: \(c = j\)
    • Same diagonal: \(\lvert r - i \rvert = \lvert c - j \rvert\)

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ij} = 1\) if a queen is placed in cell $(i,j)$, and $0$ otherwise, $\forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}$

Objective function

We want to minimize the total number of queens placed on the board:

\[\min z = \sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} \sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} x_{ij}\]

The domination constraints ensure that every cell $(i,j)$ is covered:

Coverage (Domination) Constraint:

For each cell $(i,j)$, the sum of queens in cells that can attack it must be at least $1$:

\[\sum_{(r,c) \in \mathcal{A}_{ij}} x_{rc} \geqslant 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Variable domains

\[x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Source code

The Python implementation using gurobipy to build the adjacency matrix and solve the domination problem is available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: Logical thermometers, beyond temperature
entry.content:
Image by Markus Winkler retrieved from Unsplash

The Thermometer Puzzle is an original logic puzzle where cold calculation meets spatial design. Here, capacity constraints and the physical continuity of fluids come into play.

The goal is to determine which cells of an $m \times n$ grid contain mercury. The grid is completely covered by thermometers of various shapes and lengths. Each thermometer occupies a sequence of adjacent cells (horizontally or vertically) and has a clearly identifiable base or “bulb”.

Formal description of the problem

Given an $m \times n$ grid of cells grouped into different thermometers, we must decide the fill level of each one while respecting the following physical and logical rules:

  1. Row and column requirements: The grid margins indicate exactly how many cells must be filled with mercury in each row and in each column.
  2. Continuous filling (Gravity/Thermometer physics): Thermometers are always filled from the bulb (start) towards the tail end. This implies a strict condition: if a cell contains mercury, all preceding cells in that same thermometer (closer to the bulb) must also be filled. Likewise, if a cell is empty, all subsequent cells in that thermometer must be empty.

Consider the following example of an $8 \times 8$ board:

Would you like to try solving it logically before checking its mathematical modeling?

Challenge solution

By introducing the marginal sums and the directional precedence pairs into our model, the integer optimization solver instantly reveals which cells contain mercury:

The magic of this puzzle lies in crossing the information from marginal totals with the directional rigidity of the thermometers. How do we model this apparent “fluid physics” mathematically? By using the elegance of binary linear optimization.

To model this problem, the key lies in how we represent the continuity of the mercury. Instead of creating complex numeric variables for the fill level of each thermometer, we can simply establish a logical dependency relationship between adjacent cells within the same instrument.

Index sets

  • \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, 2, \dots, m\}\): Rows of the board.
  • \(\mathcal{J} = \{1, 2, \dots, n\}\): Columns of the board.
  • \(\mathcal{A} = \{ ((i,j), (r,c)) \in (\mathcal{I} \times \mathcal{J})^2 \}\): Set of ordered cell pairs where cell $(i,j)$ is the immediate predecessor of cell $(r,c)$ within the same thermometer (that is, $(i,j)$ is one step closer to the bulb than $(r,c)$).

Parameters

  • \(R_i\): Exact number of cells that must be filled in row $i \in \mathcal{I}$.
  • \(C_j\): Exact number of cells that must be filled in column $j \in \mathcal{J}$.

Decision variables

  • \(x_{ij} = 1\) if cell $(i,j)$ is filled with mercury, and $0$ if left empty.

This is a pure feasibility problem:

Objective function

\[\min z = 0\]

The physical rules of the game translate into the following linear constraints:

Row and column totals:

The sum of filled cells in each row and column must match the values given in the margins:

\[\sum_{j \in \mathcal{J}} x_{ij} = R_i \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}\] \[\sum_{i \in \mathcal{I}} x_{ij} = C_j \quad \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Mercury continuity (Precedence):

If a cell $(r,c)$ contains mercury ($x_{rc} = 1$), its predecessor cell $(i,j)$ in the thermometer must obligatorily be filled ($x_{ij} = 1$). If the predecessor cell is empty ($x_{ij} = 0$), the successor must be empty ($x_{rc} = 0$). This bidirectional logic is modeled with a simple inequality:

\[x_{rc} \leqslant x_{ij} \quad \forall ((i,j), (r,c)) \in \mathcal{A}\]

Variable domains

\[x_{ij} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Source code

The Python implementation to solve this problem (along with the equivalent GAMS formulation proposed as an exercise) is available in the GitHub repository.

entry.title: Dominosa, Beyond Dominoes
entry.content:
Image by Mick Haupt from Unsplash

Dominosa is a fascinating logic game created by O.S. Adler in the late 19th century. Although placing domino tiles on a grid might seem simple at first glance, reconstructing the original layout of a complete domino set from a grid of revealed numbers poses a true combinatorial challenge.

The objective is to cover a rectangular board consisting of $R \times C$ numbered cells using a complete set of dominoes (from double zero $[0,0]$ to double $M$, $[M,M]$), such that each cell is covered by exactly half of a tile whose values match the numbers printed on the board.

Formal Problem Description

Given a complete set of domino tiles up to a maximum value $M$ (containing $N_d = \frac{(M+1)(M+2)}{2}$ tiles) and an $R \times C$ grid of numbers with $R \times C = 2 \cdot N_d = (M+1)(M+2)$ cells, we must place all tiles respecting the following rules:

  1. Unique tile usage: Each tile $[u, v]$ from the complete set (with $0 \leqslant u \leqslant v \leqslant M$) must be used exactly once.
  2. Complete, non-overlapping coverage: Each cell on the board must be covered by half of a single domino tile, leaving no empty spaces or overlapping tiles.
  3. Physical adjacency: A domino tile occupies exactly two adjacent cells on the board, either horizontally or vertically.
  4. Value matching: The two numbers on a domino placed over a pair of adjacent cells must match the values printed on those cells.

The key question we need to answer is: Does a valid placement of the complete domino set exist that perfectly covers the board, and how can we find it automatically?

Consider the following example (using tiles from 0 to 9 on a $10 \times 11$ board):

Do you dare to solve it logically before taking on the model?

Puzzle Solution

By solving the binary linear programming model with the given number matrix, the solver instantaneously finds the unique reconstruction of domino tiles on the board:

This logic puzzle can be formulated elegantly and systematically as a Binary Linear Programming problem. Dare to try it?

To model Dominosa as a binary linear programming problem, we identify all potential positions where a tile could be placed (adjacent edges on the board) and link each position to its corresponding domino tile based on the values of its cells.

Index Sets

  • \(\mathcal{I} = \{1, 2, \dots, R\}\): Board rows.
  • \(\mathcal{J} = \{1, 2, \dots, C\}\): Board columns.
  • \(\mathcal{M} = \{0, 1, \dots, M\}\): Possible numerical values of the domino tiles.
  • \(\mathcal{D} = \{[u, v] \in \mathcal{M} \times \mathcal{M} : u \leqslant v\}\): Set of tiles in the complete domino set (avoiding duplicates due to symmetry).
  • \(\mathcal{E} = \{ ((i,j), (r,c)) \in (\mathcal{I} \times \mathcal{J})^2 : |i-r| + |j-c| = 1, \; (i,j) < (r,c) \}\): Set of ordered pairs of adjacent cells on the board, under lexicographical order $(i,j) < (r,c) \iff i < r \lor (i = r \land j < c)$.
  • \(\mathcal{E}_{uv} = \{ ((i,j), (r,c)) \in \mathcal{E} : \{V_{ij}, V_{rc}\} = \{u, v\} \}\): Set of board positions whose numerical values match tile $[u,v]$.

Parameters

  • \(V_{ij} \in \mathcal{M}\): Number printed on cell $(i,j)$ of the board.
  • \(R, C\): Number of rows and columns of the board, where $R \times C = 2 \cdot N_d = (M+1)(M+2)$.

Decision Variables

  • \(x_{ijrc} = 1\) if a domino tile is placed on the adjacent edge $((i,j), (r,c)) \in \mathcal{E}$, and $0$ otherwise.

Since this is a feasibility problem (finding any configuration that satisfies all game rules), the objective function is arbitrary:

Objective Function

\[\min z = 0\]

We formulate the rules of Dominosa as linear constraints:

Exact coverage per cell:

Each cell $(i,j)$ on the board must be covered by exactly one domino tile (summing edges where the cell is either the first or second element of the ordered pair):

\[\sum_{(r,c) : ((i,j),(r,c)) \in \mathcal{E}} x_{ijrc} + \sum_{(r,c) : ((r,c),(i,j)) \in \mathcal{E}} x_{rcij} = 1 \quad \forall i \in \mathcal{I}, \; \forall j \in \mathcal{J}\]

Unique use of each domino tile:

Each tile $[u,v] \in \mathcal{D}$ from the complete set must be placed in exactly one of the valid positions on the board where its numbers match:

\[\sum_{((i,j), (r,c)) \in \mathcal{E}_{uv}} x_{ijrc} = 1 \quad \forall [u,v] \in \mathcal{D}\]

Variable Domain

\[x_{ijrc} \in \{0, 1\} \quad \forall ((i,j), (r,c)) \in \mathcal{E}\]

Source Code

The implementation in Python using the Gurobipy library to solve this optimization problem is available on the GitHub repository.
